Question: If I have a procedure that only requires me to stay in the hospital for a few hours instead of a full day, will that still count as hospitalisation?

Answer using only the passages above, citing pages as [p.N].

Under the definition, hospitalisation generally requires a minimum of 24 consecutive hours of inpatient care, except for specified procedures/treatments where admission can be less than 24 hours [p.13]. If your procedure meets the criteria for a Day Care Procedure — undertaken under general or local anaesthesia in less than 24 hours because of technological advancement, and would otherwise have required hospitalisation of more than 24 hours — it qualifies as a day care procedure rather than standard hospitalisation [p.5] [p.5] [p.4]. So, yes, it can be covered, but under the day care definition, not as standard 24-hour hospitalisation.

Question: How can I earn a discount on my insurance premium through the wellness program?

Answer using only the passages above, citing pages as [p.N].

You earn a discount on your premium by earning wellness points through the Star Wellness Program. The discount is based on the total points you earn: 200–350 points gives 2%, 351–600 gives 5%, 601–750 gives 7%, and 751–1000 gives 10% [p.21]. You earn points by completing wellness activities such as an Online Health Risk Assessment (50 points), submitting a Health Check-Up Report (200 points), participating in a Walkathon or Marathon (100 points), attending Yoga or Gym (100 points), achieving 10,000 average steps per day (200 points), and sharing a fitness success story (50 points) [p.29][p.27]. The program is available to insured persons aged 18 years and above [p.21]. For floater policies, weightage is applied based on family size, and for two-year policies, total points earned over the two-year period are divided by two [p.21].

Question: If I have more than one insurance policy, how does claiming work differently for an indemnity policy compared to a benefit-based policy?

Answer using only the passages above, citing pages as [p.N].

For indemnity policies, you can choose which policy to claim under, and that insurer becomes the primary insurer. If the coverage under that policy is less than the admissible claim, the primary insurer coordinates with your other insurers to settle the balance [p.25]. For benefit-based policies, on the occurrence of the insured event, you can claim from all insurers under all policies [p.25].

Answer using only the passages above, citing pages as [p.N].

If your hospital room costs more than your policy’s room rent limit, your other medical bills — including doctor fees, nursing charges, and operation theatre charges — will be paid only in the same proportion as your eligible room rent limit bears to the actual room rent charged [p.27]. The formula used is: (Eligible Room Rent limit / Room Rent actually incurred) × total Associated Medical Expenses [p.27]. The same proportionate deduction applies to room rent and all associated medical expenses [p.12]. This proportionate deduction does not apply to ICU hospitalization [p.27][p.12]. Also, this condition does not apply in hospitals where differential billing for associated medical expenses is not followed based on room rent [p.12][p.16].
